Pilgrim Badge
PIL-grim BAJ
n. (a cheap lead or pewter token sold at a shrine and worn openly, proving that a pilgrim had made the journey — the scallop of Compostela, the ampulla of Canterbury)
From pilgrim, Latin peregrinus, a foreigner, and badge, of uncertain origin — a mark worn to be seen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pilgrim badges were mass-produced at every major shrine and sold by the thousand: the scallop shell of Santiago, the little ampulla of Canterbury water said to be mixed with Becket's blood, the keys of Rome, the Virgin's image at Walsingham. They were pinned to hat or cloak, and they certified the journey to anyone who saw them. Thousands have been dredged from the Thames, thrown in on the pilgrim's return. As an object they are entirely innocent; as a practice they are the exact thing our Lord censured in another religious badge: “all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). The Christian's own mark is not worn and cannot be bought: “in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13), and “Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2Co 1:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines badge as a mark, sign, token or thing by which a person is distinguished; and token as a sign, something intended to represent or indicate another thing or event.

expand to see more

BADGE, n. A mark, sign, token or thing by which a person is distinguished, in a particular place or employment, and designating his relation to a person or to a particular occupation.

TOKEN, n. A sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing or an event.

SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance on which is engraved some image or device, used to make an impression. That which confirms, ratifies or makes stable.

EARNEST, n. First fruits; that which is in advance, and gives promise of something to come. A pledge; a part paid beforehand as a security for the whole.

AMPULLA, n. A small flask or vessel for holding liquids; in the church, a vessel for holy oil or water.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:1 — "Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven."

Eph 1:13 — "In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,"

2Co 1:22 — "Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts."

Eph 4:30 — "And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption."

Modern Corruption

The lead token proving a pilgrimage, worn where everyone could see it, and the seal that no one can.

expand to see more

The corruption is certified devotion. A badge exists to be read by other people, and once piety can be evidenced it will be collected. Our Lord's objection to the broad phylactery was not that the parchment was wrong but that the breadth was for an audience, and he states the principle before he gives any examples: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 6:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer already has a mark, and it is internal, unforgeable and given rather than earned. “and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2Co 1:22) makes the Spirit himself the down payment on what is coming. The warning attached is about grieving rather than losing him: “grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption” (Eph 4:30).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin peregrinus, a foreigner; Greek sphragizo (G4972), to seal; Greek arrabon (G728), a pledge or earnest; Greek phulakterion (G5440), a phylactery; Greek theaomai (G2300), to be gazed at.

expand to see more

Latin peregrinus — a foreigner, a traveller; whence pilgrim.

Greek theaomai (G2300) — to behold, to be seen; “to be seen of them” (Mat 6:1).

Greek sphragizo (G4972) — to seal, to mark as one's own; “ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13).

Greek arrabon (G728) — a down payment, an earnest; “and given the earnest of the Spirit” (2Co 1:22).

Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorrowful; “And grieve not the holy Spirit of God” (Eph 4:30).

Usage

"“they make broad their phylacteries” (Mat 23:5) — the badge, in its first century form."

"“ye have no reward of your Father” (Mat 6:1) — the cost of a visible piety."

"“sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” (Eph 1:13) — the mark nobody can see."
